findings.explanation: verifySignature() compares the Facebook X-Hub-Signature-256 HMAC digest to the expected value using the strict equality operator (===) instead of crypto.timingSafeEqual. String comparison with === short-circuits on the first mismatched byte, so response time leaks how many leading hex characters of the guessed signature are correct. An attacker who can measure response latency (even noisy network timing, given enough samples/averaging) can incrementally forge a valid signature byte-by-byte without knowing fbAppSecret, defeating the webhook's authenticity check and allowing spoofed Messenger events to be injected.

The GET /webhook handshake compares the caller-supplied hub.verify_token query parameter to the configured fbVerifyToken secret using ===, not crypto.timingSafeEqual. This is a timing side-channel on a secret value; exploitability is lower than the HMAC check (the endpoint is normally only invoked once at subscription setup by Meta, but it is a public unauthenticated GET route reachable by anyone who knows the webhook URL), so an attacker could still attempt a timing-based brute force of fbVerifyToken.
